title: Planet Densities: Rock or Gas?
short: A planet's mass and radius give its average density, about 4 to 5.5 g/cm³ for rocky planets and 0.7 to 1.6 g/cm³ for the giants.
trouble: Students think the biggest planets must be the densest.

blocks.html: In Planets, Moons and Small Bodies you sorted the planets into small rocky ones near the Sun and giants farther out. One number tells the two families apart and reveals what each planet is made of, even ones no spacecraft has landed on: its average density.

Density is mass divided by volume, $\rho = \frac{M}{V}$. We can measure both from far away. A planet's mass comes from the orbits of its moons or of passing spacecraft (see weighing with orbits), and its radius from its angular size and distance. A planet is close to a sphere, so $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ (volume of spheres). Then we compare with known materials: water is $1$ g/cm³, rock about $3$, iron about $8$, and hydrogen and helium far less. A planet's average density tells the mix.

Average density $= \dfrac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}$. Rocky (terrestrial) planets come out at about $4$ to $5.5$ g/cm³: rock with iron cores. The giants come out at about $0.7$ to $1.6$ g/cm³: mostly hydrogen and helium (Jupiter, Saturn) or ices (Uranus, Neptune) around small dense cores.

blocks.title: Earth's density
blocks.q: Earth's mass is $5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg and its radius $6371$ km. Find its average density.
steps: Surface rocks are only about $2.7$ to $3$ g/cm³, so the inside must be denser: Earth has an iron core.

blocks.title: A planet that floats
blocks.q: Saturn's mass is $5.68 \times 10^{26}$ kg and its radius $58{,}232$ km. Find its density.
steps: Less than water: in a big enough ocean, Saturn would float.

blocks.html: It is tempting to think the biggest planets must be the densest. The opposite is true: Jupiter is 318 times Earth's mass but about 1300 times its volume, so it is only a quarter as dense. Density compares mass with volume; size alone tells nothing. Check: Earth, a small planet, is the densest of all.
Earth's density is a little higher than it would be uncompressed, because its own weight squeezes the deep rock and iron. The Moon, at $3.34$ g/cm³, has only a small iron core.
